title: Room By Room (RBR)
pitch: Heats a house room by room — a Linux controller in the home, Zigbee thermometers and radiator valves, and a phone web app — for households and heating installers who want per-room control without a subscription.
synopsis:
Room By Room (RBR) is an open-source control system for central heating that works room by room. Each room has its own Zigbee thermometer and its own radiator valve or relay, and a controller — a small Linux mini-PC in the house — decides every few seconds whether that room should be heated, following a schedule the household sets and the temperature the room has actually reached. A relay on the boiler's demand input asks the boiler to fire only when some room wants heat.

The household uses it from a phone browser: the interface is a web app served from rbrheating.com/heat/, so there is nothing to install. It shows the rooms, their temperatures and which are heating, and it carries schedules, profiles and a calendar.

The system is deliberately self-contained. The plan lives on the controller, so the schedules keep running when the website or the internet is down; the app is a view and a remote control. Messages between the app and the controller go over MQTT through a broker in the cloud, which lets a phone reach a system behind an ordinary home router without opening a port.

Everything is plain files and ordinary parts: AllSpeak scripts (the controller written in its Python dialect, the app in its JavaScript dialect), PHP endpoints on shared hosting, Zigbee2MQTT for the radio, and one JSON file that holds the rooms and their schedules. Two installations run it today. Neither was sold, the project earns nothing, and it costs under £10 a month to run.

The project is looking for a co-maintainer, and a written continuity plan covers the day the current maintainer cannot continue.
brief:
## What it is

Room By Room is an open-source control system for central heating that works room by room. A small Linux computer in the house holds the plan and switches each radiator; Zigbee thermometers and radiator valves report and obey; and the household sets it from a web app in a phone browser, so there is nothing to install. The heating keeps running when the site or the internet is down, because the plan lives on the controller.

## Who uses it

Two private homes, run by people the maintainer knows. Neither installation was sold, so there are no paying customers, no installers under contract and no support agreements. The documentation is written for the heating trade as well as for developers, but no trade installer has taken one on commercially yet.

## Why it exists

Conventional controls heat zones or the whole house, and per-room control usually arrives as a closed, subscription product tied to one supplier. RBR is built instead from ordinary parts and plain files, with no build tools and very few dependencies. Work began in January 2022. What would be lost is a working system in two homes, a documentation set written for the trade as well as for developers, a tested handover mechanism for pointing controllers at a replacement site, and the design reasoning recorded in the repository's history and engineering notes.

## How it works

`controller.allspeak` runs on a Linux mini-PC as `controller.service`; it holds `map.json` — one shared room list, with each profile's schedules keyed by room name — re-examines every room every few seconds and drives `deviceControl.allspeak` to switch relays. Zigbee2MQTT owns the radio and `zigbee-bridge.py` translates between it and the controller. A local Mosquitto broker is bridged to the cloud broker at `rbrheating.duckdns.org`, which is how a phone reaches a house behind an ordinary router. The app is `new-ui/`, a browser PWA served from `/heat/` on the pinned AllSpeak runtime; PHP endpoints on shared hosting pair a device (`credentials.php`) and run the handover channel (`handover.php`). Heating logs and an event journal let a recorded day be replayed in `tools/rbr-studio/` without hardware.

## How to run, test and deploy it

`get-controller.sh` fetches the install pack and `rbr-setup.sh` configures the machine; `rbr-preflight.py` reports what the hardware looks like first. `tests/unit/run-unit-tests.sh`, `node tests/pwa-compile-check.js` and `node tests/docs-reader-check.js` need no broker, browser or controller; `npm run test:ui` runs the Playwright suite against a scripted MQTT client. `./deploy.sh` publishes the site, and `./deploy.sh --release` bumps the version stamp so every controller applies the update on its next hourly check. Gotchas: the pinned JavaScript runtime is older than upstream, the controller must compile as a whole, and a crash loop still shows `active` because the service restarts every five seconds.

## The estate

Repository `github.com/easycoder/rbr`, public under the personal account `@easycoder`, MIT licence. Domain and site `rbrheating.com` on shared hosting at `/home/rbrheating`, which also holds the controller update channel at `/heat/`, the account register `rbr-users.json` above the web root, and the host settings. Broker at `rbrheating.duckdns.org`, on a separate host, with its DuckDNS name. Mail at `info@rbrheating.com`, also used for recovery and for emailed backups. Controller backups, map history and event journals stay with each installation. No trademark is recorded and there are no contracts to transfer.

## The economics

No revenue and never any: nothing has been sold, and the running costs have been the maintainer's. The estate costs under £10 a month — shared hosting, the domain, the broker host and the mail account; DuckDNS is free. Hardware in each house is that household's cost. Nothing is owed: no invoices, no debts, no promised refund. An installer could charge for fitting and support, but the software has no price and there is no billing arrangement.

## The obligations

Keep `rbrheating.com` serving `/heat/` and the broker reachable, or the app stops working on every phone. Treat the account register, controller backups and event journals as personal data and keep them unpublished. Rotate credentials and per-system tokens after a transfer, and tell the households first, because a rotation unpairs every phone. Keep the MIT licence and the open-source terms. Answer support mail, or replace the address with one that is answered. Keep a named successor in the continuity plan. Promise no support contract, response time or warranty, because none exists, and exercise the handover channel against a prepared replacement site before relying on it.

## The state of play

The site, the app, the documentation and the update channel are live, and two installations run on it. Known limits are recorded in `REQUESTS.md`: the pinned runtime has no `loop`, `on failure` stops the thread, and a second blocking send can lose the first one's reply. Every system shares one MQTT account, so isolation between customers would be broker work. The documentation is drafted but unreviewed, with the installation pages and six technical pages still to write. A battery radiator-valve trial and the current-measurement phase are designed and outstanding. The continuity plan has no named successor yet.

## The first 30 days

Take the accounts in order — GitHub, registrar and DNS, hosting, DuckDNS and the broker, the mailbox. Record the successor in the continuity addendum and tell GitHub. Run the test suite, then `sudo python3 rbr-doctor.py` on a live controller. Deploy a change without `--release` and watch the controllers stay put. Speak to the two households before anything visible changes. Rotate the credentials you inherited, warning that it unpairs every phone. Exercise the handover once against a staging site. Finish the installation documentation, and only then plan the battery valve trial and the current-measurement work.

The full brief — the estate table, the reasoning behind each point, the known bugs and the detail of the first month — is published with the documentation at https://rbrheating.com/docs/#succession.
cost_description: Estimated at under 10 GBP a month in total: shared hosting and the domain for rbrheating.com, the host running the cloud MQTT broker, and the mail account for info@rbrheating.com. DuckDNS is free. The controller computers, Zigbee devices and broadband in each house are that installation's own cost, not the project's.
effort_description: Releases and deploys, support mail, keeping the two live installations working, reviewing changes, and keeping the documentation and the test suite in step. Much of the code is written by an AI agent under the maintainer's direction, so a fair share of the time goes on reviewing what it produces rather than typing.
obligations: Keep rbrheating.com serving /heat/: it is the app and the controller update channel, and every controller checks it hourly.
Keep the cloud broker reachable at rbrheating.duckdns.org, or the app stops working on every phone.
Treat rbr-users.json, controller backups and event journals as personal data: keep them local and unpublished.
Rotate credentials and per-system tokens after a transfer, and tell the households before doing it, because a rotation unpairs every phone.
Keep the code under the MIT licence and the open-source terms the continuity plan records.
Answer support and recovery mail at info@rbrheating.com, or replace it with an address that is answered.
Keep a named successor in the continuity addendum, with emergency access somewhere reachable.
Imply no support contract, response time or warranty, because none exists.
Exercise the handover channel against a prepared replacement site before relying on it.
Do not claim a household's data or pairing is unchanged if a rotation was needed.
